opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think NVIDIA has a few advantages that are pretty unique, and they really come from the fact that we sit across the entire stack.

The first is compute, obviously. Training foundation models for robotics is extremely compute-hungry, and not just for training the model itself. A huge part of the cost is generating data, and we have access to that compute at a scale that makes ambitious projects feasible.

The second, and I think the most underrated, is simulation. Robotics has a data problem that language models don't have. With LLMs you can scrape the internet, but there's no internet-scale dataset of robot motor control. You can't download joint trajectories from Wikipedia. So you have to manufacture data, and that's where simulation comes in. NVIDIA has invested for years in physics simulation and graphics, with Isaac Sim, Omniverse, and GPU-accelerated physics. We can run thousands of parallel environments, domain-randomize everything, and simulate in hours what would take a robot years in the real world. Then you combine that with generative models, essentially neural simulation, to expand diversity even further. I think of it as a data pyramid: internet-scale video at the bottom, simulation and synthetic data in the middle, and a thin but precious layer of real robot teleoperation data at the top. NVIDIA is well positioned to work on all three layers.

The third is the full-stack view, from training in the data center to simulation to deployment on the edge. A robot needs an onboard brain, and with the Jetson line, and now Thor, we can co-design the model with the hardware it will actually run on. That loop between the model, the simulator, and the chip is hard to replicate.

Finally, there's our role in the ecosystem. NVIDIA doesn't build its own humanoid robots to compete with our partners. We want to be the platform: the GR00T foundation model, the simulation tools, the compute, so that every robotics company, whether they build humanoids, arms, or autonomous machines, can build on top of it. That neutrality lets us work with practically every major player, and we learn a lot from seeing so many different embodiments and use cases.

So to sum up: compute, simulation as a data engine, full-stack hardware and software co-design, and being an enabling platform rather than a competitor. Together I think that puts us in a good position to work toward what I'd call the GPT-1 moment for robotics, and hopefully beyond it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and I'd break it down into three things.

The first is compute, obviously. People joke that we have the GPUs, and that's true, but it goes deeper than that. Robotics foundation models are incredibly data-hungry, and a huge fraction of that data is going to come from simulation, not from the real world. You can't collect a billion hours of robot teleoperation. You can, however, render it. So you need a stack where the simulator, the physics engine, the rendering, and the training loop all live on the same hardware and are optimized end to end. That's Isaac, that's Omniverse, that's the whole GPU-accelerated simulation ecosystem we've been building for years. The simulation itself is a GPU workload, so the same chips that train the model also generate its data. That flywheel is very hard for someone to replicate if they're renting compute and stitching together third-party tools.

The second is that we sit at a very unusual position in the ecosystem. We don't make the robot. We're not competing with the humanoid companies or the industrial arm companies. We want all of them to succeed, and so we can build a foundation model like GR00T that is meant to be a general brain that anyone can take, fine-tune on their embodiment, and deploy on Jetson at the edge. If you're a vertically integrated robot company, your model is tied to your hardware and your data. We get to be the platform, which means we can aggregate diversity across many embodiments, and diversity of embodiment is actually one of the key things these models need to generalize.

And the third, which I think is underrated, is the full stack from cloud to edge. A robot foundation model is useless if it only runs in a data center. It has to run in real time, on the robot, under power and latency constraints. We own the training chips, the simulation, the inference software, and the on-device compute. Very few organizations can go from a trained checkpoint to a model running on a robot at the edge without crossing a vendor boundary somewhere.

So compute plus simulation, the platform position, and the end-to-end stack. None of those alone is decisive. Together, I think they put us in a pretty unique spot to make a real attempt at a generalist robot brain.

astra-6.text:
I think NVIDIA has a pretty unique combination of capabilities. There’s the compute infrastructure—you need a lot of compute to train these models—but there’s also simulation, which is especially important for robotics. You can’t just scrape the internet for all the interactions a robot needs to learn. You need a way to generate experience, including situations that would be expensive or difficult to reproduce in the real world.

And then there’s the connection between training and deployment. You need to run the model on a physical machine, process sensor data, and act in real time. Having expertise across that whole stack lets you build a tighter loop between simulation, learning, and what actually works on the robot.

The other advantage is the ecosystem. Robotics covers many different bodies, sensors, and tasks. Working with a broad set of partners gives you a path toward building something general, rather than a model that only works for one robot in one environment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think NVIDIA has a pretty unique combination of capabilities. We have the compute to train large models, but we also have simulation, which is especially important for robotics. You can’t collect robot data at internet scale simply by putting more robots into the world. It’s expensive, it’s slow, and there are safety constraints. Simulation lets us generate experience in parallel and expose robots to a much wider range of situations.

The other advantage is the connection between those pieces: training infrastructure, simulation, and the hardware that runs the model on the robot. You can build a complete loop—generate experience, train a policy, deploy it, and use what you learn to improve the next round.

But I wouldn’t say compute alone solves robotics. The hard question is how you turn all that compute into useful experience that transfers to the real world. That’s where I think NVIDIA’s combination of capabilities becomes particularly valuable.
